title: PostgreSQL Operations
subtitle: Week 10: back up, replicate and secure a Postgres server
description: The day-two operations that keep a database safe: backups and point-in-time recovery, replication and read replicas, roles and least-privilege access, connection pooling with pgbouncer, and the maintenance routine every DBA owns.

lessons.title: Backup and Restore
lessons.body:
Backups fall into two families. A **logical backup** (`pg_dump`) reads the database through SQL and writes a consistent snapshot of the schema and data. It is portable across versions and architectures and you can restore a single table, but it is slow on very large databases and does not capture things outside the database such as roles. A **physical backup** copies the actual data files (with `pg_basebackup`), is fast and byte-for-byte, and underpins point-in-time recovery, but it is tied to the same PostgreSQL major version.

`pg_dump` has output formats: plain SQL (`-Fp`), which you replay with `psql`, and **custom** (`-Fc`), a compressed archive you restore with `pg_restore`. Custom is nearly always the better choice because `pg_restore` can be selective and parallel:

```bash
pg_dump -h db.internal -U postgres -Fc -f support.dump support
```

Restore into a fresh database and use `-j` for parallel jobs:

```bash
createdb -h db.internal -U postgres support_restore
pg_restore -h db.internal -U postgres -d support_restore -j 4 support.dump
```

A backup you have never restored is not a backup. After every restore, verify row counts on key tables, the presence of the newest records, and that grants and indexes came across. Automate that check so a silent failure in the backup job is caught before you need it.

exercises.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes a logical backup from a physical backup?
options: Logical backups read data through SQL and are portable; physical backups copy the data files and underpin point-in-time recovery
Logical backups are always faster than physical ones
Physical backups cannot be restored to another server
Logical backups include the roles and tablespaces that physical backups miss
exercises.explain: pg_dump is logical and portable; pg_basebackup is a physical file copy used for PITR and tied to the same major version.
exercises.hint: One reads through SQL, the other copies files.

exercises.prompt: Write a `pg_dump` command that saves the `support` database to `support.dump` in custom (compressed) format.
exercises.explain: Custom format is compressed and lets pg_restore run selectively and in parallel, unlike plain SQL.
exercises.hint: Custom format is the -Fc flag.

exercises.prompt: When using `pg_restore`, which flag names the target database to restore into?
options: -d
-F
-f
-j
exercises.explain: -d names the destination database. -f selects an output file, -F sets format, and -j sets the number of parallel jobs.
exercises.hint: It is the same letter psql uses to pick a database.

exercises.prompt: Write a `pg_restore` command that restores `support.dump` into database `support_restore` using 4 parallel jobs.
exercises.explain: Parallel restore with -j speeds up large custom-format archives by loading tables concurrently.
exercises.hint: Parallel jobs use the -j flag.

lessons.title: Point-in-Time Recovery and WAL
lessons.body:
Between backups the database is never standing still. The **write-ahead log (WAL)** records every change before it is written to the main files, so a crash can be replayed forward. That same WAL makes **point-in-time recovery (PITR)** possible: restore a base backup, then replay archived WAL up to a chosen moment - say, ten seconds before the bad `DELETE`.

To enable it, turn on WAL archiving. Set `archive_mode = on` and an `archive_command` that copies each completed WAL segment somewhere safe, for example `archive_command = 'cp %p /backups/wal/%f'`. Then take a **base backup** with `pg_basebackup`, which records the WAL position it started from.

To recover, stop the server, restore the base backup files, create a `recovery.signal` file (PostgreSQL 12+), and set a target:

| setting | stops replay at... |
| --- | --- |
| `recovery_target_time` | a wall-clock timestamp |
| `recovery_target_xid` | a transaction id |
| `recovery_target_lsn` | a WAL location |
| `recovery_target_name` | a named restore point |

Start the server; it replays WAL and stops at the target, then continues on a new timeline. Keep the archive on storage separate from the database, or losing the disk loses the backups too.

exercises.prompt: What is the write-ahead log (WAL) for?
options: Recording every change before it reaches the data files, so a crash can be replayed and PITR is possible
Storing a second copy of the whole database
Caching query results for the planner
Compressing backups automatically
exercises.explain: WAL is the durability and recovery mechanism: redo recorded in the log can rebuild the data files after a crash and be replayed to a chosen point.
exercises.hint: It is written ahead of the actual data change.

exercises.prompt: Put these steps of a point-in-time recovery in the order you would perform them.
items: Enable WAL archiving with archive_mode and archive_command
Take a base backup with pg_basebackup
Restore the base backup files onto the server
Set recovery_target_time and create the recovery.signal file
Start the server so it replays WAL up to the target
exercises.explain: Archiving must be on before the base backup, the base backup is the starting point, then you restore it, set the target, and start to replay WAL to that moment.
exercises.hint: You cannot recover to a point unless archiving was on and a base backup exists.

exercises.prompt: Which recovery setting stops WAL replay at a specific wall-clock timestamp?
exercises.explain: recovery_target_time sets a timestamp target; replay stops once the database reaches that moment, the classic undo-the-bad-DELETE move.
exercises.hint: It is recovery_target_ plus the word for time.

exercises.prompt: Where must the WAL archive live for a PITR strategy to be safe?
options: On storage separate from the database server
On the same disk as the data directory for low latency
Only in the server's memory
Inside the base backup itself
exercises.explain: If the archive shares the disk with the database, losing that disk loses both. Off-server storage is what makes recovery possible.
exercises.hint: Think about what happens when the database disk fails.

lessons.title: Replication and Read Replicas
lessons.body:
Replication keeps a second server continuously in step, giving you a standby for failover and a replica to serve reads. **Streaming (physical) replication** ships the WAL byte stream and produces an exact, read-only copy of the whole cluster. A standby connects using `primary_conninfo` in `postgresql.conf` and stays in recovery until you promote it. **Logical replication** ships row-level changes for selected tables through publications and subscriptions; it works across major versions and lets the subscriber be writable, but it does not replicate DDL or sequences.

To promote a standby, run `pg_ctl promote -D /var/lib/postgresql/data` (or just `pg_ctl promote`). It stops replay, becomes read-write, and continues on a new timeline so it can never rejoin the old primary by accident.

For **read scaling**, point report queries at a streaming replica. Be aware of **replication lag**: a replica is eventually consistent, so a read straight after a write may not see that write. Applications that must read their own writes should send those queries to the primary.

```sql
SELECT client_addr, state, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication;
```

Monitor lag with the `pg_stat_replication` view on the primary. Always test failover by actually promoting a replica, not just by reading the configuration.

exercises.prompt: What is the main difference between streaming and logical replication?
options: Streaming ships the WAL byte stream for the whole cluster; logical ships row changes for selected tables and allows a writable subscriber
Streaming only copies the schema, logical copies data
Logical replication requires the same major version
Streaming replication cannot be used for failover
exercises.explain: Physical streaming is a byte-for-byte WAL copy tied to the major version; logical replication is row-based, selective, and version-flexible.
exercises.hint: One is WAL-level, the other is row-level.

exercises.prompt: What happens when you promote a standby?
options: It stops replay, becomes read-write, and continues on a new timeline
It deletes its data and re-syncs from the primary
It becomes read-only permanently
It erases the WAL archive
exercises.explain: A promoted standby leaves recovery, accepts writes, and moves to a new timeline so it cannot accidentally follow the old primary again.
exercises.hint: Promotion turns a follower into the leader.

exercises.prompt: Write the command to promote a standby whose data directory is `/var/lib/postgresql/data`.
exercises.explain: pg_ctl promote tells the standby to leave recovery and become a primary. The -D flag points at its data directory.
exercises.hint: pg_ctl has a promote subcommand.

exercises.prompt: An application writes a row then immediately reads it from a read replica. What can go wrong?
options: Replication lag means the replica may not have the write yet, so the read returns nothing
The replica rejects all reads during replay
The write is applied twice
The read blocks until the primary confirms it
exercises.explain: Replicas are eventually consistent. Read-your-own-writes must go to the primary, or the application must tolerate lag.
exercises.hint: Replicas are only eventually consistent.

lessons.title: Roles, Privileges and Security

exercises.prompt: What does the principle of least privilege mean here?
options: Each role gets only the privileges its work requires, and no SUPERUSER unless essential
Every application shares one powerful role for simplicity
All roles can read every table by default
Privileges are granted to the public schema
exercises.explain: Least privilege limits the blast radius of a compromised or buggy application: it can touch only what it was explicitly granted.
exercises.hint: Grant the minimum, not the maximum.

exercises.prompt: Write a `GRANT` giving the `analyst` role SELECT on the table `reporting.orders`.
exercises.solution: GRANT SELECT ON reporting.orders TO analyst;
exercises.explain: This grants read-only access to one table. The analyst also needs USAGE on the reporting schema to reach it.
exercises.hint: GRANT privilege ON object TO role.

exercises.prompt: What does `pg_hba.conf` control?
options: Which hosts, databases and authentication methods are allowed to connect
Which columns a role may read
How much memory the server uses
The order of WAL replay during recovery
exercises.explain: pg_hba.conf is the host-based access list: for each combination of connection type, address, database and user, it names the authentication method.
exercises.hint: Its name means host-based authentication.

exercises.prompt: Put these checks in the order a connection passes through them, from outside in.
items: pg_hba.conf accepts the host, database and auth method
The role must have LOGIN and CONNECT on the database
The role must have USAGE on the schema
The role must hold the privilege on the table
exercises.explain: You are admitted at the door (pg_hba), then allowed into the database, then the schema, and finally the individual table - failure at any layer blocks you.
exercises.hint: Start with the network door, end with the object itself.

lessons.title: Connection Pooling and Maintenance Routine
lessons.body:
Every PostgreSQL connection is a forked process using a few megabytes of memory, so `max_connections` is a hard ceiling you cannot raise for free. Applications that open a connection per request quickly exhaust it. **pgbouncer** sits between clients and the server and multiplexes many client connections onto a small pool of real ones.

pgbouncer has pooling modes: **session** (a server connection is held for the whole client session), **transaction** (returned after each transaction - the best default for most apps), and **statement**. Transaction mode is efficient but forbids session-level state such as a session `SET` or an advisory lock held across statements, so know your application before choosing it.

A DBA's routine keeps the server healthy. Watch:

| check | view |
| --- | --- |
| active vs idle connections | `pg_stat_activity` |
| table and index bloat | `pg_stat_user_tables` and `pgstattuple` |
| blocking locks | `pg_locks` joined to `pg_stat_activity` |
| replication lag | `pg_stat_replication` |
| autovacuum progress | `pg_stat_progress_vacuum` |

An operations checklist: confirm last night's backup restored cleanly in a test; verify replication lag is near zero; check for long-running or blocked queries; confirm autovacuum is keeping up; and alert on connection counts approaching `max_connections` before users hit `too many clients` errors.

exercises.prompt: Which pgbouncer pooling mode returns the server connection to the pool after every transaction?
options: Transaction pooling
Session pooling
Statement pooling
Direct pooling
exercises.explain: Transaction pooling is the usual default: it gives high reuse while allowing multi-statement transactions, but session-level state cannot survive between transactions.
exercises.hint: The pool is held for the duration of one transaction.

exercises.prompt: What limits how many direct client connections PostgreSQL will accept?
options: max_connections
shared_buffers
work_mem
autovacuum_max_workers
exercises.explain: max_connections is the hard cap, and each slot costs memory. Raising it recklessly is why pooling is preferred over a huge connection count.
exercises.hint: The setting name contains the word connections.

exercises.prompt: Which system view lists current connections and what each backend is doing?
exercises.explain: pg_stat_activity shows one row per backend with its state, current query, wait event and timings - the first place to look for idle-in-transaction or blocked sessions.
exercises.hint: It is a pg_stat_ view whose name means activity.

exercises.prompt: Put this daily operations checklist in a sensible order.
items: Confirm last night's backup restored cleanly in a test
Verify replication lag is near zero
Check for long-running or blocked queries
Confirm autovacuum is keeping up with bloat
exercises.explain: Recovery safety first, then replication health, then live query and lock health, then maintenance and capacity - a routine that catches the biggest risks first.
exercises.hint: Start with whether you could recover, end with capacity headroom.
